categories.content: A data lakehouse keeps data in open formats on cheap storage and lets many engines work on the same tables. This landscape maps the layers you need and the projects and products that fill them.

subcategories.content:
The landscape has two tabs. They share storage, table format, catalog, orchestration, BI and semantic layers, and differ in how data is computed:

  • Data Lakehouse with SQL Query Engine: people and tools work in SQL, and a query engine serves them.
  • Data Lakehouse with Analytics Processing Engine: people work in Python or DataFrames, and a processing engine runs their code.

Many teams run both on the same tables.

Start at the table format. It decides which catalogs and engines can work together. An item can appear in more than one layer. White boxes are open source according to the license GitHub reports for the listed repository; gray boxes are everything else.
Open a pull request at data-inconsistencies/landscape. Being listed is not an endorsement.

categories.content: Engines and tools where SQL is the main interface.

subcategories.content: Tools that bring data in from databases, applications, files and event streams, in batches or continuously.
Tools that turn raw tables into modeled ones with SQL, on a schedule or continuously.
Engines that answer SQL queries. Some read open tables in place, some keep their own storage, and many do both.

categories.content: Engines and libraries where Python, DataFrames or other code is the main interface.

subcategories.content: Python libraries and frameworks that load data into the lakehouse.
Distributed engines and DataFrame libraries that process data, from one machine to a large cluster.
In-process engines and libraries that query tables and files from code.
Native execution layers that speed up an engine such as Spark without changing user code.

categories.content: A catalog tells engines which tables exist, where their current metadata is, and who may use them.

subcategories.content: Catalogs that can register Apache Hudi tables.
Catalogs that can serve Apache Iceberg tables, often through the Iceberg REST API.
Catalogs that can register Delta Lake tables.
Branches, commits and merges for data, so changes can be tested in isolation and rolled back.
Discovery, lineage, quality and governance for people, above the technical catalog.

categories.content: Formats turn files in storage into tables that several engines can read and write safely.

subcategories.content: Specifications that add transactions, schema evolution and time travel to files in a lake.
Tools that let a table written in one format be read as another.
File and in-memory layouts that table formats and engines are built on.
Cloud services and self-hosted systems that store objects, usually with an S3-compatible API.
Hadoop file storage and systems compatible with it.
Layers between compute and storage that cache data or present object storage as a file system.
Storage for continuously arriving data that feeds lakehouse tables.

categories.content: Orchestrators decide what runs, when, and in which order.

subcategories.content: Tools organized around the datasets they produce, so lineage and freshness are first-class.
Tools organized around tasks and workflows.

categories.content: How people see and explore the data.

subcategories.content: Dashboards and reports built mainly in a visual interface.
Dashboards, notebooks and data apps kept as code and reviewed like code.

categories.content: One definition of metrics and relationships, shared by every tool that asks.

subcategories.content: Semantic layers that are part of a commercial product.
Semantic layers with an open source repository.
